newsitem.title: FRANCE: France considers voting system reform.
newsitem.headline: France considers voting system reform.

text.p: France may reform its parliamentary election system to add an element of proportional representation, Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Friday.
The change could strengthen minor parties like the far-right National Front, which failed to win a single seat in 1993 in the last general election despite polling 12.5 percent of the popular vote.
"I think that a debate should be opened on the modernisation of our institutions, for example, on our election system," Juppe said in an interview to be published in the daily Le Figaro on Saturday.
"A good election system should free up a majority of the government -- that's the Gaullist in me that is speaking -- but at the same time it should enable minorities to be heard."

The daily Le Monde said earlier Juppe told parliamentary floor leaders that he had for some time been weighing an electoral reform, which is also advocated by the opposition socialists and communists.

The most fervent supporters of reform are smaller parties like the anti-immigrant National Front and the divided ecologist movement, which have been kept out of parliament by the current single-member constituency system, which favours larger groups.
Bruno Megret, a senior National Front leader, welcomed an electoral reform but said in a statement that it showed how frightened the centre-right government was of his party's rise in public support.

Some major party leaders also backed reform including National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin of the ruling Gaullist party and Claude Goasguen, general secretary of the Union for French Democracy, the junior partner in the governing coalition.
"We will at some point have to find a way of ensuring that all major political currents are represented in parliament," Seguin told a ruling Gaullist party meeting.
"Within the UDF, we are not hostile to such a discussion," Goasguen told reporters at a party conference in La Baule.
Under the current system, a candidate must win more than half the votes in the first round to be elected outright to the National Assembly. Otherwise the two top candidates go on to a run-off.

Politicians have argued over the voting system since the late president Charles de Gaulle abolished proportional representation in 1958 to restore political stability after an era of revolving-door cabinets dependent on shifting alliances among a large number of parties.

The late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand restored proportional representation for the 1986 general election, but the conservative government of President Jacques Chirac, then prime minister, reverted to the constituency system the following year.

Juppe gave no details of how he would structure a reform but parliamentary floor leaders said deputies might be elected by proportional representation in the most populated regions while single-member constituencies remained in rural areas.
